table.text: This study has been approved by the ethics board of the School of Psychology of the University of Sussex (ER/ASF25/5).
The idea that we are endowed with the potential to unconsciously alter our subjective experience and distort reality -even momentarily -to meet the goals at hand is not novel.
table.header: Testing the Relationship between Phenomenological Control related to Illusion Sensitivity

table.text: The goal is to recruit around 500 adult English speakers using Prolific.

Methods Participants Five hundred adult English speakers (Mean age = 38.6, SD = 13.1, range: [18, 75], 49.4% of women) were recruited via Prolific (www.prolific.com) and completed the study on a desktop device.
table.formatted: Methods Participants Five hundred adult English speakers (Mean age = 38.6, SD = 13.1, range: [18, 75], 49.4% of women) were recruited via Prolific (<ref type="url" target="www.prolific.com">www.prolific.com</ref>) and completed the study on a desktop device.

table.text: Participants were first presented with an explanatory statement and the consent form, and could proceed by pressing a button to confirm they had read and understood the information.

1 Eligibility was implemented using Prolific's screening filters for participants whose first or primary language was English, which departs from the Stage 1 description (see Deviations From Registration).
Following the informed consent, participants were presented with demographic questions (gender, education level, age, and ethnicity).
Participants were asked to put on their headphones and await further auditory instructions.
Once the 10 suggestions were completed, participants were asked to rate their subjective experiences and response to each suggestion on a 6-points Likert scale (from 0-5).
Participants completed a total of 1,340 trials, with the experiment lasting approximately 55 minutes.
The study involved three visual illusions, in which participants were instructed to respond as quickly as possible without making errors.
In a subsequent exercise, participants were instructed: "Open your eyes.
In another task, participants were instructed to press the spacebar six times.

Eligibility was implemented using Prolific's screening filters, which admitted participants whose first or primary language was English; the Stage 1 wording did not reflect this intended recruitment criterion and was an error in the Stage 1 manuscript.
In our paradigm, participants were explicitly motivated to respond as quickly and accurately as possible, effectively incentivizing them to actively inhibit or "resist" the illusory interference.

Instead, the failure rate may reflect how the check was implemented: although the auditory instruction, delivered with eyes closed, stated that the "PLEASE WAIT" message would appear "a little later", the screen appeared as soon as the recording ended (i.e., as participants were told to open their eyes), disappeared after 10 seconds, and only recorded presses made while it was displayed.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> The idea that we are endowed with the potential to unconsciously alter our subjective experience and distort reality -even momentarily -to meet the goals at hand is not novel.

> The goal is to recruit around 500 adult English speakers using Prolific.

> Methods Participants Five hundred adult English speakers (Mean age = 38.6, SD = 13.1, range: [18, 75], 49.4% of women) were recruited via Prolific (www.prolific.com) and completed the study on a desktop device.

> Participants were first presented with an explanatory statement and the consent form, and could proceed by pressing a button to confirm they had read and understood the information.

> 1 Eligibility was implemented using Prolific's screening filters for participants whose first or primary language was English, which departs from the Stage 1 description (see Deviations From Registration).

> Following the informed consent, participants were presented with demographic questions (gender, education level, age, and ethnicity).

> Participants were asked to put on their headphones and await further auditory instructions.

> Once the 10 suggestions were completed, participants were asked to rate their subjective experiences and response to each suggestion on a 6-points Likert scale (from 0-5).

> Participants completed a total of 1,340 trials, with the experiment lasting approximately 55 minutes.

> The study involved three visual illusions, in which participants were instructed to respond as quickly as possible without making errors.

> In a subsequent exercise, participants were instructed: "Open your eyes.

> In another task, participants were instructed to press the spacebar six times.

> Eligibility was implemented using Prolific's screening filters, which admitted participants whose first or primary language was English; the Stage 1 wording did not reflect this intended recruitment criterion and was an error in the Stage 1 manuscript.

> In our paradigm, participants were explicitly motivated to respond as quickly and accurately as possible, effectively incentivizing them to actively inhibit or "resist" the illusory interference.

> Instead, the failure rate may reflect how the check was implemented: although the auditory instruction, delivered with eyes closed, stated that the "PLEASE WAIT" message would appear "a little later", the screen appeared as soon as the recording ended (i.e., as participants were told to open their eyes), disappeared after 10 seconds, and only recorded presses made while it was displayed.

Ethics approval statement:

> This study has been approved by the ethics board of the School of Psychology of the University of Sussex (ER/ASF25/5).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

For example, the codebook documents ``Illusion_Type``, ``Illusion_Strength``, ``Illusion_Difference`` while the data has `Participant`, `Recruitment`, `Experiment_StartDate`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.
report: This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.
We examined 2 codebook/README/label sources and 1006 data columns across 30 files.

**A codebook was found and parsed (6 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents ``Illusion_Type``, ``Illusion_Strength``, ``Illusion_Difference`` while the data has `Participant`, `Recruitment`, `Experiment_StartDate`. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.**

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 2 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: open-document lock files (2). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

#### Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an `renv.lock`/`DESCRIPTION` for R, a `requirements.txt` for Python). No `install.packages()` calls were found in any of the code files.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 1006 columns across 30 data files.
#### Issues Identified

42 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 30 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: The idea that we are endowed with the potential to unconsciously alter our subjective experience and distort reality -even momentarily -to meet the goals at hand is not novel.
The goal is to recruit around 500 adult English speakers using Prolific.

Methods Participants Five hundred adult English speakers (Mean age = 38.6, SD = 13.1, range: [18, 75], 49.4% of women) were recruited via Prolific (www.prolific.com) and completed the study on a desktop device.
Participants were first presented with an explanatory statement and the consent form, and could proceed by pressing a button to confirm they had read and understood the information.

1 Eligibility was implemented using Prolific's screening filters for participants whose first or primary language was English, which departs from the Stage 1 description (see Deviations From Registration).
Following the informed consent, participants were presented with demographic questions (gender, education level, age, and ethnicity).
Participants were asked to put on their headphones and await further auditory instructions.
Once the 10 suggestions were completed, participants were asked to rate their subjective experiences and response to each suggestion on a 6-points Likert scale (from 0-5).
Participants completed a total of 1,340 trials, with the experiment lasting approximately 55 minutes.
The study involved three visual illusions, in which participants were instructed to respond as quickly as possible without making errors.
In a subsequent exercise, participants were instructed: "Open your eyes.
In another task, participants were instructed to press the spacebar six times.

Eligibility was implemented using Prolific's screening filters, which admitted participants whose first or primary language was English; the Stage 1 wording did not reflect this intended recruitment criterion and was an error in the Stage 1 manuscript.
In our paradigm, participants were explicitly motivated to respond as quickly and accurately as possible, effectively incentivizing them to actively inhibit or "resist" the illusory interference.

Instead, the failure rate may reflect how the check was implemented: although the auditory instruction, delivered with eyes closed, stated that the "PLEASE WAIT" message would appear "a little later", the screen appeared as soon as the recording ended (i.e., as participants were told to open their eyes), disappeared after 10 seconds, and only recorded presses made while it was displayed.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 10 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:10, File = c("_apa_title.qmd", "paper/R1/manuscript.qmd", 
"preprocessing.R", "1_cleaning.qmd", "1_cleaning.R", "2_analysis.qmd", 
"2_analysis.R", "manuscript_trackedchange.qmd", "paper/Stage2/manuscript.qmd", 
"paper/Stage2_R1/manuscript.qmd"), "Runs after" = c("—", "—", 
"—", "preprocessing.R", "preprocessing.R", "1_cleaning.qmd, 1_cleaning.R, preprocessing.R", 
"1_cleaning.qmd, 1_cleaning.R, preprocessing.R", "2_analysis.qmd, 2_analysis.R", 
"2_analysis.qmd, 2_analysis.R", "2_analysis.qmd, 2_analysis.R"
), Basis = c("none", "none", "none", "dependency", "dependency", 
"dependency", "dependency", "dependency", "dependency", "dependency"
)), row.names = c(NA, -10L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited. **6 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 10 scripts: 6 ran without error, 4 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}

"", "", "undefined_variable", "undefined_variable", "", "", ""
), "Time (s)" = c(0.6, 2.9, 1.3, 10, 9.9, 4.6, 5, 2.5, 2.7, 3.2
)), row.names = c(NA, -10L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Undefined-variable errors**

**3 scripts failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

text.text: Author roles were classified using the Contributor Role Taxonomy (CRediT; https://credit.niso.org/) as follows:
text.formatted: Author roles were classified using the Contributor Role Taxonomy (CRediT; <ref type="url" target="https://credit.niso.org/">https://credit.niso.org/</ref>) as follows:

text.text: Visual Illusions are an interesting type of stimuli highlighting the ease with which our phenomenological conscious experience can become dissociated from physical reality.
Their robust and reliable effect makes them useful stimuli to explore how perception is constructed and shaped, and several theoretical models have been put forth to explain how they work.

In particular, illusions have been reframed using a predictive coding account of perception (e.g., Notredame et al., 2014; Nour & Nour, 2015) in which the brain optimally combines, using some flavour of Bayesian inference, perceptual inputs with prior knowledge to make sense of ambiguous environments (Friston, 2010). Such computational model(s) propose to conceptualize illusions as stimuli providing weak or conflicting sensory evidence (Gershman et al., 2012; Sundareswara & Schrater, 2008) that bias perception toward prior knowledge.
text.formatted: In particular, illusions have been reframed using a predictive coding account of perception (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Notredame et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Nour & Nour, 2015)</ref> in which the brain optimally combines, using some flavour of Bayesian inference, perceptual inputs with prior knowledge to make sense of ambiguous environments <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Friston, 2010)</ref>. <ref type="bibr">Such computational model(s)</ref> propose to conceptualize illusions as stimuli providing weak or conflicting sensory evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Gershman et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Sundareswara & Schrater, 2008)</ref> that bias perception toward prior knowledge.

text.text: In other words, the weight of priors, in the form of perceptual knowledge about the world (e.g., internalized rules of perspective) is amplified when the sensory input is confusing.

For instance, in the Müller-Lyer illusion, we "compute" the two (actually identical) lines as being of different lengths because the line flanked with converging fins is misinterpreted as being further away (Notredame et al., 2014).
text.formatted: For instance, in the Müller-Lyer illusion, we "compute" the two (actually identical) lines as being of different lengths because the line flanked with converging fins is misinterpreted as being further away <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Notredame et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In this context, measuring sensitivity to illusion can be operationalized as indexing the parameters of the Bayesian inference process (e.g., prior precision).
These accounts also provide a compelling framework to explain existing findings reporting interindividual variability in the sensitivity to illusions.

Indeed, several studies suggest a potential link with psychopathology, in particular schizophrenia (Costa et al., 2023) and autism (Gori et al., 2016), in which the reported lower sensitivity to illusions has been attributed to a diminished influence of top-down processes such as prior knowledge (Mitchell et al., 2010) and a greater emphasis on (i.e., precision of) sensory information (Palmer et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Indeed, several studies suggest a potential link with psychopathology, in particular schizophrenia <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Costa et al., 2023)</ref> and autism <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Gori et al., 2016)</ref>, in which the reported lower sensitivity to illusions has been attributed to a diminished influence of top-down processes such as prior knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Mitchell et al., 2010)</ref> and a greater emphasis on (i.e., precision of) sensory information <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Palmer et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence beyond psychopathology also suggests variability in the general population, potentially correlated with personality traits such as agreeableness and honesty-humility (Makowski et al., 2023), as well as cognitive abilities (Shoshina & Shelepin, 2014).
text.formatted: Evidence beyond psychopathology also suggests variability in the general population, potentially correlated with personality traits such as agreeableness and honesty-humility <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Makowski et al., 2023)</ref>, as well as cognitive abilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Shoshina & Shelepin, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: However, the exact nature of this interindividual variability and its potential origin remains unclear.

The somewhat mixed evidence in the literature regarding its generalizability and strength could be related to the variety of the paradigms used and the type of processes being mobilised (Makowski et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The somewhat mixed evidence in the literature regarding its generalizability and strength could be related to the variety of the paradigms used and the type of processes being mobilised <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Makowski et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, traditional methods frequently focus on participant's experience by prompting them to assess the difference between two identical targets, estimate the target's physical properties, or adjust the targets to match a reference stimulus (Todorović, 2020).
text.formatted: Indeed, traditional methods frequently focus on participant's experience by prompting them to assess the difference between two identical targets, estimate the target's physical properties, or adjust the targets to match a reference stimulus <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Todorović, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Relying on metacognitive judgments about one's subjective experiences adds an additional layer to the measure that might not be desired when attempting to measure illusion sensitivity.

Moreover, paradigms often face challenges in diversifying the illusory effects (i.e., using multiple stimuli to experimentally manipulate the strength of the illusion) and the illusion types (i.e., using various illusions, such as Müller-Lyer, Ebbinghaus, Delboeuf which might rely on a different admixture of mechanisms), hindering the potential of obtaining a comprehensive, valid, and reliable measure of illusion sensitivity.

The "Illusion Game" paradigm (Makowski et al., 2023) has been recently developed to measure illusion sensitivity to various illusion types through its behavioural impact (on response time and error rate) in a perceptual decision task (where participants have to respond as fast as possible; e.g., "which of the left or right circles is bigger").
text.formatted: The "Illusion Game" paradigm <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Makowski et al., 2023)</ref> has been recently developed to measure illusion sensitivity to various illusion types through its behavioural impact (on response time and error rate) in a perceptual decision task (where participants have to respond as fast as possible; e.g., "which of the left or right circles is bigger").

text.text: The stimuli for different classical illusions are created using the Pyllusion software (Makowski et al., 2021), which allows researchers to modulate the strength of the illusion as a continuous dimension, independently from the difficulty of the perceptual task.
text.formatted: The stimuli for different classical illusions are created using the Pyllusion software <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Makowski et al., 2021)</ref>, which allows researchers to modulate the strength of the illusion as a continuous dimension, independently from the difficulty of the perceptual task.

text.text: This paradigm, inspired by psychophysics, lends itself to the computational modelling of illusion sensitivity through its interference effect -an effect that disrupts an individual's ability to accurately discriminate between perceptual stimuli.
This approach aims to bypass some of the metacognitive processes involved in other paradigms, offering a more direct and objective measure of how illusions influence perceptual judgment.

Interestingly, the fact that inter-individual variability in illusion sensitivity seems to persist in this task suggests that it is not solely explained by metacognitive ability differences, and gives rise to the following question: is the variability in illusion sensitivity related to lowlevel perceptual processes (e.g., baseline precision of perceptual priors), or rather to the ability to actively control and "resist" the illusion in order to achieve the task at hand (higher-level modulation of the perceptual inference parameters).

If the latter is true, then illusion sensitivity measured in contexts with strong task-demand characteristics, e.g., in paradigms where participants' performance is explicitly or implicitly assessed (i.e., where there is an incentive to downplay the illusion effect) might correlate with one's ability to alter one's subjective experience following suggestions -a mechanism referred to as "phenomenological control".
The idea that we are endowed with the potential to unconsciously alter our subjective experience and distort reality -even momentarily -to meet the goals at hand is not novel.

While this phenomenon has been historically often studied under the label of "hypnotisability" -the tendency to alter our conscious experience to match external demands (Lush et al., 2021), the term "phenomenological control" (PC) has been recently introduced to disconnect this concept from the potentially negative associations with hypnosis and the misconception that a hypnotic context is necessary for responding to imaginative suggestions (Dienes et al., 2022).
text.formatted: While this phenomenon has been historically often studied under the label of "hypnotisability" -the tendency to alter our conscious experience to match external demands <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Lush et al., 2021)</ref>, the term "phenomenological control" (PC) has been recently introduced to disconnect this concept from the potentially negative associations with hypnosis and the misconception that a hypnotic context is necessary for responding to imaginative suggestions <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Dienes et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: To encourage the empirical exploration of our ability and tendency to alter our phenomenological experience and further accelerate investigations away from the hypnotic context, Lush et al. (2021) adapted the Sussex-Waterloo Scale of Hypnotisability (SWASH, Lush et al., 2018) by removing all its references to hypnosis, to measure trait phenomenological control.
text.formatted: To encourage the empirical exploration of our ability and tendency to alter our phenomenological experience and further accelerate investigations away from the hypnotic context, <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Lush et al. (2021)</ref> adapted the Sussex-Waterloo Scale of Hypnotisability (SWASH, <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Lush et al., 2018)</ref> by removing all its references to hypnosis, to measure trait phenomenological control.

text.text: This newly developed phenomenological control scale (PCS) consists of 10 imaginative suggestions followed by subjective ratings for each suggestion and has demonstrated validity in online experiments (Lush et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This newly developed phenomenological control scale (PCS) consists of 10 imaginative suggestions followed by subjective ratings for each suggestion and has demonstrated validity in online experiments <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Lush et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, Lush et al. (2022) did test for a relationship between PC and illusion sensitivity using the Müller-Lyer illusion (in which the arrangement of the arrowheads flanking two lines makes them appear as having different lengths), and reported evidence in favour of an absence of correlation between the two measures.
text.formatted: Interestingly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Lush et al. (2022)</ref> did test for a relationship between PC and illusion sensitivity using the Müller-Lyer illusion (in which the arrangement of the arrowheads flanking two lines makes them appear as having different lengths), and reported evidence in favour of an absence of correlation between the two measures.

text.text: This finding was interpreted as indicative of the cognitive impenetrability of illusions, implying that the effect is driven by low-level processes and therefore not influenced by top-down mechanisms such as PC.

Note that both prior-knowledge and phenomenological control are considered top-down processes, but the cognitive impenetrability hypothesis suggests that the processes at stake for the illusions happen at a lower-encapsulated-level (in the form of perceptual priors).

The goal of this study is thus to replicate the results from Lush et al. (2022) pointing to an absence of a relationship between phenomenological control and illusion sensitivity, by generalising them to a different illusion paradigm that encompasses other illusion types.
text.formatted: The goal of this study is thus to replicate the results from <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Lush et al. (2022)</ref> pointing to an absence of a relationship between phenomenological control and illusion sensitivity, by generalising them to a different illusion paradigm that encompasses other illusion types.

text.text: Additionally, we also explored the relationship between psychoticism, as a proxy for schizophrenia, and illusion sensitivity to assess the potential impact of lower-level effects-such as weak priors observed in individuals with schizophrenia (Costa et al., 2023)-on sensitivity to illusions.
text.formatted: Additionally, we also explored the relationship between psychoticism, as a proxy for schizophrenia, and illusion sensitivity to assess the potential impact of lower-level effects-such as weak priors observed in individuals with schizophrenia <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Costa et al., 2023)</ref>-on sensitivity to illusions.

text.text: These analyses may offer evidence clarifying whether inter-individual variability in illusion sensitivity is driven by lower-level perceptual mechanisms or higher-level cognitive processes (Table 1).
text.formatted: These analyses may offer evidence clarifying whether inter-individual variability in illusion sensitivity is driven by lower-level perceptual mechanisms or higher-level cognitive processes (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: In line with Lush et al. (2022), we hypothesise that there will be evidence supporting the absence of a relationship between PC and VI sensitivity.
text.formatted: In line with <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Lush et al. (2022)</ref>, we hypothesise that there will be evidence supporting the absence of a relationship between PC and VI sensitivity.

text.text: Based on Makowski et al. (2023) and prior work on weak priors in schizophrenia, we hypothesise that higher psychoticism scores will be negatively associated with VI sensitivity.
text.formatted: Based on <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Makowski et al. (2023)</ref> and prior work on weak priors in schizophrenia, we hypothesise that higher psychoticism scores will be negatively associated with VI sensitivity.

text.text: The goal is to recruit around 500 adult English speakers using Prolific.
This sample size is based on the ones used in Lush et al., 2021 and Lush et al., 2022 that we aim at replicate.
text.formatted: This sample size is based on the ones used in <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Lush et al., 2021 and</ref> <ref type="bibr">Lush et al., 2022</ref> that we aim at replicate.

text.text: Bayesian correlations will be conducted using the BayesFactor::correlationBF() function, with a 8 139 140 141 medium prior (r-scale = 1/3), separately for: 1) PC scores and VI sensitivity (error rate and IES), across all three illusion types; and 2) Psychoticism facet scores from the PID-5 and VI sensitivity scores, across all three illusion types.
For the PC-VI sensitivity relationship, we will interpret BF₁₀ ≤ 1/3 as evidence against a relationship, in line with Lush et al. (2022).
text.formatted: For the PC-VI sensitivity relationship, we will interpret BF₁₀ ≤ 1/3 as evidence against a relationship, in line with <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Lush et al. (2022)</ref>.

text.text: For the psychoticism-VI sensitivity relationship, BF₁₀ > 3 will be interpreted as evidence supporting a relationship, following findings by Makowski et al. (2023).
text.formatted: For the psychoticism-VI sensitivity relationship, BF₁₀ > 3 will be interpreted as evidence supporting a relationship, following findings by <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Makowski et al. (2023)</ref>.

text.text: If there is no evidence for a PC-VI relationship across all three illusions, it would support the hypothesis that VI sensitivity is independent from PC.
If a negative association is found between psychoticism and VI sensitivity, it may suggest a low-level perceptual basis for inter-individual differences in illusion sensitivity.

Theory That Could Be Shown Wrong by the Outcomes The cognitive impenetrability of visual illusions, which posits that illusion sensitivity is driven solely by low-level processes and is not influenced by top-down mechanisms such as phenomenological control.
Conversely, a lack of association with psychoticism would challenge the view that low-level perceptual alterations underlie illusion sensitivity in non-clinical populations.

Methods Participants Five hundred adult English speakers (Mean age = 38.6, SD = 13.1, range: [18, 75], 49.4% of women) were recruited via Prolific (www.prolific.com) and completed the study on a desktop device.
text.formatted: Methods Participants Five hundred adult English speakers (Mean age = 38.6, SD = 13.1, range: [18, 75], 49.4% of women) were recruited via Prolific (<ref type="url" target="www.prolific.com">www.prolific.com</ref>) and completed the study on a desktop device.

text.text: 1 Out of these participants, 2.8% reported having a doctoral degree, 18.2% masters degree, 49.6% a bachelors degree, 27.4% a high school degree and 2% other qualifications.
Participants were first presented with an explanatory statement and the consent form, and could proceed by pressing a button to confirm they had read and understood the information.
This study has been approved by the ethics board of the School of Psychology of the University of Sussex (ER/ASF25/5).
Following the exclusion steps (see Results and Figure A1), 295 participants (Mean age = 38.1, SD = 12.9, 48.8% women) were retained in the registered analysis.

Sensitivity analyses addressing deviations from the registered protocol were conducted on a larger sample of 468 participants (Mean age = 38.7, SD = 13.2, 48.7% women), of whom 458 were analysed for each illusion (see Deviations From Registration).

1 Eligibility was implemented using Prolific's screening filters for participants whose first or primary language was English, which departs from the Stage 1 description (see Deviations From Registration).
Procedure The experiment's setup follows the born-open principle (De Leeuw, 2023), and all its related material is available at https://github.com/RealityBending/IllusionGamePhenomenologicalControl.
text.formatted: Procedure The experiment's setup follows the born-open principle (De Leeuw, 2023), and all its related material is available at <ref type="url" target="https://github.com/RealityBending/IllusionGamePhenomenologicalControl">https://github.com/RealityBending/IllusionGamePhenomenologicalControl</ref>.

text.text: The online experiment, implemented entirely using JsPsych (De Leeuw, 2015), has its code stored on
GitHub and leverages the power of the platform to host the experiment for free.
Participant's raw data files (containing identifiers) were stored in a private OSF repository, but anonymized using a publicly available preprocessing script.
The resulting anonymized data, and the analysis reports, are available, ensuring the transparency and reproducibility of all the analysis steps.
Following the informed consent, participants were presented with demographic questions (gender, education level, age, and ethnicity).
Although these variables were not directly analyzed in the current study, they were used to provide a detailed and thorough description of the sample and to maximize data reusability.
Participants then underwent the Phenomenological Control Scale (PCS) and the Illusion Game task (IG) in a counterbalanced order.
Participants were asked to put on their headphones and await further auditory instructions.

The PCS procedure started with a recorded introduction explaining that a series of tests would be applied to evaluate how experiences can be created through imagination, followed by 10 suggestions in a fixed order (see Lush et al., 2021), such as "now extend your arms ahead of you, with palms facing each other, hands about a foot apart" and "as you sit comfortably in your chair with your eyes closed, a picture of two balls will be displayed on the computer screen".
text.formatted: The PCS procedure started with a recorded introduction explaining that a series of tests would be applied to evaluate how experiences can be created through imagination, followed by 10 suggestions in a fixed order (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Lush et al., 2021</ref>), such as "now extend your arms ahead of you, with palms facing each other, hands about a foot apart" and "as you sit comfortably in your chair with your eyes closed, a picture of two balls will be displayed on the computer screen".

text.text: Once the 10 suggestions were completed, participants were asked to rate their subjective experiences and response to each suggestion on a 6-points Likert scale (from 0-5).
The Phenomenological control score was computed by averaging the scores from the 10 scales.

The Illusion Game task used in the current study is an adaptation of the one used in Makowski et al. (2023) to make it shorter, in which participants must make perceptual judgments (e.g., "which red line is the longer") as quickly and accurately as possible.
text.formatted: The Illusion Game task used in the current study is an adaptation of the one used in <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Makowski et al. (2023)</ref> to make it shorter, in which participants must make perceptual judgments (e.g., "which red line is the longer") as quickly and accurately as possible.

text.text: It included 3 illusion types, namely Ebbinghaus, Müller-Lyer, and Vertical-Horizontal (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: It included 3 illusion types, namely Ebbinghaus, Müller-Lyer, and Vertical-Horizontal (see Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: In the original Illusion Game, 10 visual illusions were presented in two sets, following a practice trial, and separated by two short questionnaires.
Participants completed a total of 1,340 trials, with the experiment lasting approximately 55 minutes.
In the current procedure, only three illusions were used, selected based on the original study's findings that these illusions most strongly contribute to illusion sensitivity.
The study involved three visual illusions, in which participants were instructed to respond as quickly as possible without making errors.

Each illusion included two manipulated parameters: strength (e.g., the angle of the outward-or inward-pointing arrow-like fins in the Müller-Lyer illusion) and difficulty (e.g., the difference in line lengths in the Müller-Lyer illusion).
The procedure encompassed 2 sets of 80 trials for each illusion type, preceded by a practice trial for each illusion.

Each set included, in a random order, the 3 blocks of illusion types, in which trials were separated by a fixation cross, temporally (uniformly sampled duration of 500 -1000ms) and spatially jittered (around the centre of the screen in a radius of a 1 cm) to attenuate its potential usefulness as a reference point.

After each illusion type block, an arbitrary score was presented (computed as a scaled Inverse Efficiency Score) as a gamification mechanism to increase motivation to perform to the best of one's abilities.
To mitigate for the potential variability in the speed/accuracy trade-off, the instructions emphasized with equal weight to be fast and to avoid errors.

For each illusion type, two continuous dimensions were orthogonally manipulated namely task difficulty and illusion strength, so that each trial corresponds to a unique combination, providing an objectively correct answer for each trial.
The use of these manipulations allows concise, standardised reporting of illusion parameters and ensures our stimuli are fully reproducible (see Makowski et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The use of these manipulations allows concise, standardised reporting of illusion parameters and ensures our stimuli are fully reproducible (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Makowski et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Task difficulty corresponds to the difficulty of the perceptual decision (e.g., if the task is to select the longest red line, task difficulty corresponds to how the lines are objectively different).
Illusion strength corresponds to the degree to which the illusion elements (e.g., the black arrow lines in Müller-Lyer) are interfering with the aforementioned task.

Note that the illusion effect can be either "incongruent", making the task more difficult by biasing perceptual decisions toward the incorrect response or "congruent", making the task easier by biasing decisions toward the correct response (e.g., in the Müller-Lyer illusion, if the outwards-facing arrowheads are placed on the longer line, identifying which line is the longest becomes easier).
Participants responded with a key arrow (left vs. right; or up vs. down), and their reaction time (RT) and accuracy were recorded.
Visual illusion sensitivity was measured as the average error rate in the incongruent condition, and separately for the 3 illusion types.

Although the error rate is arguably a crude score, which does not take into account the effect of varying illusion strength, the interaction with task difficulty and the possible adjustments in response strategy (speed-accuracy trade off), it is also the most simple and easy to reproduce, hence its usage as our primary outcome for the current registered report.
As a secondary exploratory outcome, the Inverse Efficiency Score [IES; Townsend and Ashby (2014)] was computed.
This metric incorporates both speed and accuracy by dividing the mean reaction time of correct responses by the proportion of correct responses, separately for each illusion.

The two sets of 3 illusion blocks were separated by 2 short questionnaires acting as a break, namely the IPIP-6 (Sibley et al., 2011), measuring 6 personality traits with 24 analogue scales items, and the PID-5 (Krueger et al., 2011), measuring 5 maladaptive personality traits with 25 Likert scales items.
text.formatted: The two sets of 3 illusion blocks were separated by 2 short questionnaires acting as a break, namely the IPIP-6 <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Sibley et al., 2011)</ref>, measuring 6 personality traits with 24 analogue scales items, and the PID-5 <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Krueger et al., 2011)</ref>, measuring 5 maladaptive personality traits with 25 Likert scales items.

text.text: These questionnaires were included as a way of providing a break between the two cognitively taxing blocks and maintain paradigmatic consistency with previous studies (Makowski et al., 2023).
text.formatted: These questionnaires were included as a way of providing a break between the two cognitively taxing blocks and maintain paradigmatic consistency with previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Makowski et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, the psychoticism subscale of the PID-5 was used to examine the correlation between maladaptive traits and illusion sensitivity, evaluating the existence of the link proposed in previous studies (Costa et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Additionally, the psychoticism subscale of the PID-5 was used to examine the correlation between maladaptive traits and illusion sensitivity, evaluating the existence of the link proposed in previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Costa et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The phenomenological control scale included several attention checks to identify problematic participants.

The task consisted of various auditory and visual exercises; at the outset, participants heard a voice say "Hello" and were asked to select the corresponding phrase from multiple options (i.e., "Hello", "Goodbye", "How are you", "Thank you").
Selecting an incorrect response indicated inattention to auditory stimuli.
In a subsequent exercise, participants were instructed: "Open your eyes.
You will see only two balls on the screen… just two balls".
However, three differently coloured balls were displayed.
If a participant selected the response "No Balls Were Presented", it suggested they failed to attend to both the auditory instruction and the visual stimuli.
In another task, participants were instructed to press the spacebar six times.
Pressing it fewer than five times within the allotted time indicated a failure to follow the auditory instructions.
Participants who failed any one of these were to be excluded from further analysis (see Deviations From Registration).
Finally, the reliability of the PCS was assessed by computing Cronbach's alpha of its items (Cronbach, 1951).
text.formatted: Finally, the reliability of the PCS was assessed by computing Cronbach's alpha of its items <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Cronbach, 1951)</ref>.

text.text: Outliers in the Illusion Game were identified based on participants' performance.
Specifically, any participant exhibiting an error rate greater than 45% for any illusion type was considered to be responding at chance level (i.e., randomly) and flagged accordingly.
If this level of performance occurred in the first block, the entire participant was excluded from analysis, as it suggests a failure to properly engage with the task.
However, if the elevated error rate was observed only in the second block, this was interpreted as a loss of engagement or motivation (e.g., boredom due to task repetition).

In such cases, only the second block was discarded, Next, to determine whether the Mild and Strong Illusion Strength groups could be collapsed for further analysis, Bayesian correlations were computed between them for each illusion and outcome measure.
If these correlations were sufficiently high (r > .50, Cohen, 2013), the groups were collapsed and outcomes recomputed across all relevant trials (i.e., by averaging across these groups).

In addition to a discrepancy between the recruitment criterion and its description in the Stage 1 manuscript (see Participant Eligibility), we identified three issues during analysis that could affect the validity of the registered exclusions: an attention check that was failed by a disproportionate number of participants, trials with implausible response times, and a small number of participants who appeared to have misunderstood the task instructions.
These three issues are described below and were addressed together in an unregistered analysis, used as a sensitivity analysis (see Sensitivity Analyses).
Participant Eligibility.The Stage 1 manuscript specified that adult native English speakers would be recruited.

Eligibility was implemented using Prolific's screening filters, which admitted participants whose first or primary language was English; the Stage 1 wording did not reflect this intended recruitment criterion and was an error in the Stage 1 manuscript.
As a result, 59 of the 500 recruited participants (43 of the 295 participants in the registered analysis) did not report English as their first language.
The effect of this deviation was evaluated by restricting the registered analysis to native English speakers (N = 252; see Sensitivity Analyses and Table A1 and Table A2).
Phenomenological Control.The registered protocol specified that participants failing any of three attention checks in the PCS would be excluded.

text.text: To ensure the robustness of these findings to various analysis decisions, we additionally computed the correlations with variant scores of the illusion game, namely with Mild and Strong analysed separately for all scores, and with outcomes computed separately for each difficulty level (i.e., Easy and Hard).

With Mild and Strong analysed separately, 9 of the 12 PCS correlations supported the null and 3 were inconclusive; across the 36 difficultyspecific PCS correlations, 29 supported the null and 7 were inconclusive.
No PCS correlation supported a relationship.

For psychoticism, one correlation supported a relationship in both variants: IES for the Ebbinghaus illusion in the Strong condition (Mild and Strong separate: ρ=0.17, B F10 =11.4 ; Easy trials: ρ=0.17, B F10 =11.2 ), which was positive, i.e., in the direction opposite to the registered hypothesis.
All other psychoticism correlations supported the null or were inconclusive.

Finally, PCS correlated with the error rate ( B F10 =6.32 ) and IES ( B F10 =4.94 ) in the congruent condition of the Ebbinghaus illusion (Figure 2); as the congruent condition does not index illusion sensitivity, these correlations were not part of the registered tests and should be interpreted with caution.

This study aimed to replicate previous findings indicating (1) an absence of a relationship between visual illusion sensitivity and phenomenological control (Lush et al., 2022), and (2) the existence of a negative relationship between illusion sensitivity and psychoticism (Makowski et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This study aimed to replicate previous findings indicating (1) an absence of a relationship between visual illusion sensitivity and phenomenological control <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Lush et al., 2022)</ref>, and (2) the existence of a negative relationship between illusion sensitivity and psychoticism <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Makowski et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Although both PC and illusion susceptibility can be conceptualized as top-down processes, our results suggest they operate at different levels of the cognitive hierarchy.
The perceptual priors assumed to drive illusion sensitivity might be organized in a modular and encapsulated fashion.

Consequently, even individuals with a high capacity to alter their subjective experience in response to goals or expectations (high PC) do not appear to exert high-level, goal-directed control over these low-level perceptual inferences.
In practice, this suggests that the trait capacity to manipulate one's phenomenology is insufficient to override the behavioural interference of these illusions.
The inconclusive result for the Vertical-Horizontal illusion, however, indicates that this conclusion cannot be extended to all three illusions tested.

In contrast to our registered hypothesis, we found no evidence of an association between Conceptually, we could hypothesize that the task-performance on any single illusion is driven by a combination of illusion-specific factors (e.g., the particular perceptual properties and localized prior-systems engaged by that specific visual configuration) and illusion-general factors (an overarching, trait-level characteristic tapped into during illusory perceptual interference).
When analyzing specific illusions in isolation, the illusion-specific factors might overweigh the common component, potentially masking associations with broad personality constructs.

However, this assumption is challenged by the fact that the internal consistency (i.e., the intercorrelation) between the three illusions in our sample was remarkably low, inconsistent at first glance with the notion of a common "illusion sensitivity" factor.

This lack of coherence might Another important consideration for contextualizing these findings lies in the specific cognitive demands of the Illusion Game and the distinction between trait and state phenomenological control.
In our paradigm, participants were explicitly motivated to respond as quickly and accurately as possible, effectively incentivizing them to actively inhibit or "resist" the illusory interference.

This voluntary, goal-directed attempt to suppress a visual bias likely mobilizes distinct cognitive mechanisms compared to contexts where individuals are simply invited to passively experience or contemplate an illusion.
In such contemplative settings, individuals might even implicitly magnify the illusory effect for aesthetic or psychological engagement.

Furthermore, the present study measured trait phenomenological control, the baseline capacity for altering subjective experience, but did not provide an explicit induction or suggestion to alter the perception of the stimuli (i.e., state phenomenological control).

The registered analyses were repeated in the unregistered analysis described in Deviations From Registration, which addressed the issues identified during analysis: the space bar check was not applied, and extreme trials and participants with extreme result from a compounding of issues related to both the low number of illusions, as well as the specific measurement indices utilized.

Indeed, it is important to underline that the above findings and hypotheses are predicated on one critical assumption: that the outcome measures used in the current study (error rate and IES) are valid and sensitive indices to the individual differences in illusion sensitivity.

Previous studies that successfully detected relationships with personality traits, such as Makowski et al. (2023), utilized indices derived from participant-specific parameters extracted from group-level hierarchical Bayesian General Additive Models (GAMs).
text.formatted: Previous studies that successfully detected relationships with personality traits, such as <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Makowski et al. (2023)</ref>, utilized indices derived from participant-specific parameters extracted from group-level hierarchical Bayesian General Additive Models (GAMs).

text.text: In contrast, the current pre-registered analysis intentionally relied on rather crude summary measures.
This critical methodological trade-off regarding how perceptual interference is quantified was adopted as complex computational models, while sensitive, carry considerable drawbacks.

For instance, they are computationally challenging and complex, and the resulting individual indices are not easily reproducible and replicable (as the estimates are inherently dependent on a bespoke parent model estimated from a specific dataset).

Moreover, they are inherently limited by the appropriateness of the parent model as an accurate representation of the underlying data-generating process, which as noted by Makowski et al. (2023), is not yet established.
text.formatted: Moreover, they are inherently limited by the appropriateness of the parent model as an accurate representation of the underlying data-generating process, which as noted by <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Makowski et al. (2023)</ref>, is not yet established.

text.text: In particular, while the GAMs used are great models to describe complex, potentially non-linear, patterns and relationships, they did not account for the interaction between speed and accuracy, which might be an important aspect of illusion-related perceptual interference effects.

But while our chosen summary metrics provided a straightforward, reproducible index of performance, collapsing the variance across task difficulty, illusion strength, and speed-accuracy trade-offs might have stripped away the nuanced resolution required to detect the subtle, low-level individual differences associated with personality-level characteristics.
The sensitivity of the tests was psychopathological constructs must bridge the gap between reproducibility and modeling sensitivity.

This could involve utilizing computational frameworks that explicitly model the speed-accuracy trade-off, such as Drift Diffusion Models (DDMs), to disentangle true perceptual bias from response impulsivity.

Furthermore, developing standardized, multi-illusion batteries will be essential for successfully isolating a common, trait-level "illusion sensitivity" factor from the noise of illusion-specific variance.
Until such high-resolution, reliable metrics are established, the subtle links between subclinical maladaptive traits and predictive coding parameters might remain difficult to capture.

Most failures (177 of 189) recorded no presses at all, which argues against dropped key presses (which would produce partial counts).

Most of these participants (181 of 189) passed the other two checks, and in the sample used for the sensitivity analyses (N = 468), the scores of participants who failed the space bar check on the remaining PCS items were not lower than those of participants who passed it (M = 2.49 vs.
2.28; B F10 =2.90 ), suggesting that failures did not reflect general inattention.

Instead, the failure rate may reflect how the check was implemented: although the auditory instruction, delivered with eyes closed, stated that the "PLEASE WAIT" message would appear "a little later", the screen appeared as soon as the recording ended (i.e., as participants were told to open their eyes), disappeared after 10 seconds, and only recorded presses made while it was displayed.
Participants who were still reorienting after opening their eyes, or who pressed during the instruction, would therefore have been recorded as not pressing at all.
We therefore repeated the analyses without the space bar check as part of the unregistered analysis.

In this sample (the 481 participants who passed the first two PCS checks), the registered Illusion Game criteria fully excluded 8 participants on the basis of error rate and 5 on the basis of RT (none of whom were flagged by both criteria), and removed the second block of 7 participants (who were retained), leaving 468 participants.
Illusion Game.Two unregistered exclusions were applied to the Illusion Game data in the unregistered analysis.
First, the Stage 1 protocol referred to the removal of problematic trials but did not specify a criterion.

text.text: For the primary outcome (error rate), the correlation between PCS and illusion sensitivity provided evidence for the null for the Müller-Lyer (ρ=0.04, B F10 =0.19 ) and Ebbinghaus illusions (ρ=0.02, B F10 =0.14 ), and was inconclusive for the Vertical-Horizontal illusion (ρ=0.08, B F10 =0.38 ).
For the secondary outcome (IES), 3 of the 4 PCS tests supported the null and 1 was inconclusive (Müller-Lyer, B F10 =0.45 ).
The correlations between psychoticism and error rates all supported the null ( B F10 =0.14 -0.17), as did 2 of the 4 IES tests, while the other 2 were inconclusive ( B F10 =0.40 and B F10 =0.92 ).
None of the registered tests therefore supported the hypothesised negative association between psychoticism and illusion sensitivity.
Figure2
Applying the registered criteria without the space bar check (N = 468) led to the same conclusions for the primary outcome.

For the secondary outcome (IES), two tests of the Vertical-Horizontal illusion (Mild) were inconclusive rather than supporting the null (PCS: B F10 =0.38 ; psychoticism: B F10 =0.74 ), and one test of the relationship between psychoticism and IES provided evidence for a relationship (Vertical-Horizontal, Strong: B F10 =3.21 ; Table A2), although in the direction opposite to the registered hypothesis.

Restricting the registered analysis to native English speakers (N = 252), as specified in the Stage 1 protocol, also led to the same conclusions for the primary outcome, with evidence for the null for all three illusions (Vertical-Horizontal: B F10 =0.25 ).

None of these changes altered the conclusions for the primary outcome: in the unregistered analysis, PCS was unrelated to error rates for the Müller-Lyer ( B F10 =0.11 ) and Ebbinghaus illusions ( B F10 =0.11 ), the evidence for the Vertical-Horizontal illusion remained inconclusive ( B F10 =0.42 ), and all psychoticism-error rate correlations supported the null ( B F10 =0.11 -0.20).
The classification of a few tests of the secondary outcome (IES) lying close to the evidential thresholds varied between versions, but none supported a relationship in the unregistered analysis.

For the primary outcome (error rate), registered Bayesian correlation analyses provided evidence against a relationship between phenomenological control and sensitivity to two of the three illusions tested (Müller-Lyer and Ebbinghaus), whereas the evidence for the third (Vertical-Horizontal) was inconclusive, partly supporting the first hypothesis.
For psychoticism, the data favoured the absence of an association with error rates, contrary to the second hypothesis, whereas the evidence for IES was mixed.

These conclusions were robust to the data quality issues identified during analysis: an unregistered analysis that addressed them, with a larger sample, did not change any conclusion for the primary outcome.
The present findings partly replicate Lush et al.

For the primary outcome, we obtained evidence against a relationship between trait phenomenological control (PC) and sensitivity to the Müller-Lyer and Ebbinghaus illusions, whereas the evidence for the Vertical-Horizontal illusion was inconclusive.

Crucially, while previous research relied largely on subjective metacognitive judgments, our use of the Illusion Game paradigm extends this null finding to a direct, behavioral measure of perceptual interference.
This pattern is consistent with the cognitive impenetrability of these illusions under the present task conditions.
visual illusion sensitivity and the psychoticism facet of the PID-5; for the primary outcome, the Bayes factors favoured the absence of an association rather than being merely uninformative.

This result was unexpected, given the literature linking schizophrenia-spectrum traits and schizotypy to reduced susceptibility to visual illusions, a phenomenon often attributed to the reduced precision of perceptual priors within predictive coding frameworks.

One possible contributor is the limited variability of psychoticism in our general-population sample: scores were low on average (M = 0.48 on a 0-3 scale) and positively skewed, with most participants scoring near the bottom of the scale (FigureA2).
Such a restricted range limits the ability to detect associations.
However, this discrepancy may also be driven by how individual differences were operationalized in the current study.

For instance, whereasMakowski et al. (2023) measured sensitivity across an aggregate of 10 different visual illusions, the current procedure was streamlined to include only three, and the relationship with psychoticism was analyzed for each illusion individually.

Notably, the unregistered analysis, with a larger sample, led to the same conclusions for the primary outcome.
